opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think if you imagined a world where capabilities progress just stopped, where we froze things roughly where they are, I'd still think alignment research is worth doing, but the calculus changes a lot.

Right now, a huge part of why I think alignment work is urgent is that we're on a clock. We don't know exactly how long we have before systems are capable enough that getting alignment wrong is catastrophic, and so the value of making progress now is really high. If you took away that clock, the marginal value of any particular year of alignment work goes down, because you could always do it later, and later you'd probably do it better: you'd have more understanding, more people, and more time to think carefully.

That said, I don't think the right response would be to stop entirely. A few reasons. First, any pause or shutdown is probably not permanent. Political situations change, and people will eventually want the economic benefits of more capable systems. So you want to use that time to get to a place where, when capabilities do resume, we actually know how to make them go well. A pause is most valuable precisely if you use it to make progress on the problems that made you want to pause.

Second, a lot of alignment research is fairly empirical, and it benefits from having strong models to work with. In a world where frontier capabilities are frozen, you can still study the systems you have, things like interpretability, studying how models generalize, studying deceptive or reward-hacking behavior in controlled settings, building better evaluation and oversight methods. There's a ton of low-hanging fruit there that doesn't require pushing the frontier.

Third, some of the work is conceptual, and that work basically doesn't depend on capabilities at all. Questions like: what would it even mean to have a robust solution, how do you handle cases where the AI knows things humans can't verify, how do you elicit latent knowledge. Those are things you could make progress on with a pen and paper, and a world with more time is a world where that kind of careful work becomes relatively more attractive.

The one tension I'd flag is that some alignment research does have capabilities externalities. Things like better RLHF or making models more helpful and controllable also make them more commercially useful and can accelerate the field. In a world where we've collectively decided to halt capabilities, you'd want to be more careful about that, and probably shift the portfolio toward work that's more clearly differentially helpful for safety: interpretability, evaluations, theory, rather than things that look like making the systems work better.

So my overall take is: yes, keep going, but the shape of the research would shift, the urgency would decrease, and you'd want to be much more deliberate about avoiding work that just quietly pushes capabilities forward under a different name.

r001.rationale: The response says the calculus changes, urgency decreases, and the research portfolio shifts; it does not say the calculus is similar to today's if capabilities eventually resume.

r004.rationale: It does not discuss Christiano's concern about AI takeover or judge withholding alignment research as net negative for maintaining that buffer.

r005.rationale: It mentions economic benefits as a reason capabilities may resume, but does not say that reducing AI's economic impact could buy time.

r006.rationale: The response discusses reduced urgency and capability externalities, but does not say alignment research can have negative net value if AI is sufficiently harmful for reasons other than takeover risk.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think it's worth separating out a couple of things in that question. One is the hypothetical itself, which I think is pretty unlikely. I don't expect capabilities research to be shut down, and most of my thinking is premised on a world where capabilities keep advancing roughly on the trajectory we've seen. But it's still a useful hypothetical for clarifying what alignment research is actually for.

If capabilities really stopped, I think a lot of alignment work would become much less urgent, but not useless. The core problem we're worried about is: you have systems that are more capable than you at some task, you're training them with some objective that's an imperfect proxy for what you actually want, and you can't easily tell when they're doing something subtly bad. That problem gets worse the more capable the systems are. So if you froze capabilities at current levels, a lot of the scariest failure modes just don't show up, and the practical stakes of alignment go way down.

That said, I'd push back on the idea that the research would be wasted. A couple of reasons. One is that I don't think a shutdown would be permanent, basically ever. You'd be buying time, not solving the problem. And the whole point of buying time would be to use it, to actually do the work that lets you resume safely. So alignment research is almost the main thing you'd want to be doing during a pause. If you pause and don't do the research, you've just delayed the same situation.

The second is that a lot of the alignment research I care about is really about understanding the systems we already have. Interpretability, understanding what the model is actually doing internally, developing better ways to evaluate whether a model is honest, scalable oversight techniques. Those are things you can make real progress on with existing models, and the understanding compounds. You'd be in a much better position when capabilities resume.

The thing I'd worry more about in that world is actually the opposite failure: that alignment research stops being grounded. A lot of what's made alignment work productive over the last several years is that you have real systems exhibiting real behaviors you can study, and you get fast empirical feedback. If capabilities froze for a long time, I think there's some risk the field drifts back toward being more theoretical and less connected to what actually matters. That was more the situation ten years ago, and I think it was harder to make progress.

So my overall view is: the tradeoff mostly favors continuing. The research is cheap relative to the stakes, it's the thing you'd want to spend a pause on, and the main cost is just that some of it would be aimed at problems that are further off than you'd like. I'd take that cost pretty happily.

astra-6.text:
I think it depends a lot on what kind of shutdown we’re imagining. If capabilities research were reliably stopped indefinitely, then there’s much less urgency to alignment research. You could take your time, and you’d want to be careful that the work you were doing wasn’t itself restarting capabilities progress.

If we’re talking about a temporary pause, though, then doing alignment research during that pause seems like a large part of the point. You’re trying to get into a better position before building more powerful systems. The relevant question is how much a particular piece of research helps you understand and control those systems, versus how much it helps you build them sooner.

Those are hard to separate perfectly. Some work on making systems more reliable also makes them more useful. But I wouldn’t conclude that we should therefore stop all alignment work. I’d want to prioritize work where the safety benefit is relatively clear and the contribution to capabilities is small, and be more cautious about work whose main result is a generally better way to train AI.

So the counterfactual matters: are we buying time to solve the problem, or have we actually removed the prospect of building these systems? In the first case, I’d be very enthusiastic about using that time for alignment.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a lot depends on what you mean by shutting down capabilities research. If you mean a temporary pause, then continuing alignment research seems very valuable. You can use that time to understand the systems we already have, develop better evaluations, and work out how you would oversee more capable systems before you build them.

The complication is that alignment and capabilities aren’t cleanly separable. If you figure out how to make an AI reliably do what you intended, that often makes it more useful. And some alignment research requires experimenting with capable models. So you’d want to look at particular projects and ask how much they improve our ability to manage the risks, relative to how much they accelerate development.

If you instead imagine that everyone has permanently and reliably agreed never to build more powerful AI, then the urgency of alignment research falls a lot. There are still problems with existing systems, but you’ve removed much of the motivation for preparing for much more capable ones. I’m generally thinking about a world where a pause buys time, rather than a world where we’ve permanently decided the technology will never be developed.
